events.text: A letter comes from the far south. The last of the twelve who trained beside you in the outer courtyard has died. The letter is from a great-granddaughter. She writes that he talked about you to the end. Mostly about the time you fell in the well. You are the only one left who remembers the well.

choices.text: Travel south for the rites

effects.log: The family does not know who you are. You bow at the tablet with the others. Afterwards you tell the children about the well. They laugh in the right places.

choices.text: Burn incense where the courtyard stood

effects.log: The courtyard is a cabbage field now. You light the incense between two rows. The smoke goes straight up. No wind. Good.

choices.text: Write the twelve names down before you forget

effects.log: You get eleven at once. The twelfth takes until dawn. It was the one who pushed you in the well.

events.text: Young swordsmen in the market are all doing the same strange stance. Back foot turned out, blade held low like a hoe. They call it the Willow Gate Style. It is forty years old and very fashionable. When you were young it would have got a person killed. You watch them practise. It still might.

choices.text: Study it properly for a season

effects.log: It is cleverer than it looks. The low blade hides the true line. You find the flaw anyway. You keep it to yourself.

choices.text: Show them why the back foot is wrong

effects.log: You tap one ankle with a stick. The swordsman sits down hard. The others stare. Next day half of them have changed their feet.

choices.text: Shrug and buy dumplings

effects.log: Every style was new once. Yours was. The dumplings, at least, are the same as ever.

events.text: At an inn a merchant asks your name. You tell it. He laughs so hard he spills his wine. That master, he says, lived in his grandfather's time. Everyone knows the old monster is dead. He pats your shoulder kindly and advises you to pick a name with less baggage.

choices.text: Agree and pick a new name

effects.log: You call yourself Old Kim from the Hills. Old Kim gets a free drink. The famous master never got free drinks.

choices.text: Bend his wine cup with one finger

effects.log: The cup folds like paper. The merchant stops laughing. He pays for your room, your supper, and something like an apology.

choices.text: Ask what else everyone knows about you

effects.log: You learn you were eight feet tall, born in a thunderstorm, and allergic to plums. Two of these are wrong.

events.text: Drums on the river road again. Two warlords want the same valley. You have seen this valley change hands twice. The first time the soldiers had spears. The second time crossbows. This time they have something new: long tubes on carts that cough fire and stone. The village headman asks what you think will happen.

choices.text: Tell him: the valley outlasts them all

effects.log: "Hide the seed rice and the daughters, send the sons to the hills, come back for the harvest." It worked twice. It works again.

choices.text: Lead the villagers up the mountain path

effects.log: Two hundred people, four goats, one very loud grandmother. You get them all over the ridge before the first fire-tube coughs.

choices.text: Go and look at the fire-tubes

effects.log: Iron, powder, a spark. No qi at all. A child could fire one. You stand in the reeds for a long time after that.

events.text: Nothing has happened for a month. You have meditated. You have swept the yard twice. You have counted the roof tiles: three hundred and eleven, one cracked. You are, for the first time in a hundred years, bored. It is a strange, itchy feeling, like a cough you cannot reach.

choices.text: Take up a new art: calligraphy

effects.log: Your first characters are terrible. Wonderful. Something to be bad at again. You buy more paper.

choices.text: Learn to cook properly

effects.log: You burn the first pot of rice. The second is edible. The tenth is good. The neighbours start dropping by at supper.

choices.text: Fix the cracked tile, then sit with it

effects.log: Three hundred and eleven tiles, none cracked. You watch the light move across them all afternoon. Not bored. Something better.

events.text: A stall girl sells you pears. Her laugh stops you dead. It is the laugh of a friend you buried eighty years ago. Same gap in the teeth, same snort at the end. She notices you staring and asks if the pears are bad.

choices.text: Ask about her family

effects.log: Her great-grandmother was a sword dancer. Yes, that one. She asks how you knew. You say you guessed from the laugh.

choices.text: Buy every pear on the stall

effects.log: She thinks you are mad. You carry two baskets of pears home and give them out on the road. It seemed the right thing.

choices.text: Say nothing and walk on, smiling

effects.log: Some people do not end. They go on in a laugh at a fruit stall. You did not know that before.

events.text: In a pawnshop window hangs a sword with a nicked guard. You know the nick. You made it, a hundred years ago, blocking a spear on a bridge. You lost the sword in the river that night. The pawnbroker wants fifteen taels and swears it belonged to a famous general.

choices.text: Buy it back (15 taels)

effects.log: It is lighter than you remember. Or you are stronger. It still pulls slightly left. You laugh out loud in the street.

choices.text: Tell the pawnbroker the true story

effects.log: He listens politely, then raises the price to twenty. "A famous master's sword is worth more than a general's."

choices.text: Leave it for someone who needs a sword

effects.log: A poor youth buys it a month later, you hear. Good. It always did prefer to be used.

events.text: Old men in the teahouse argue about the new rankings of masters. You are not on it. You were removed thirty years ago, presumed dead. A scholar reads the list aloud. Number nine is a sword saint you taught to hold chopsticks. Number four is a person you have never heard of.

choices.text: Find out who number four is

effects.log: A spear master from the north, sixty years old. Good wrists, by all accounts. You feel something you have not felt in decades: curiosity.

choices.text: Write to number nine to say well done

effects.log: The reply comes in a month: three pages, terrible handwriting, very happy. Still holds chopsticks wrong.

choices.text: Enjoy being dead

effects.log: Nobody challenges a dead person. You sleep late, eat well, and nobody asks you for anything. Highly recommended.

events.text: Your knee clicks on cold mornings. It has done so since a fall in your twentieth year. Qi has healed every other wound you ever took. This one it never touched. A hundred winters, the same small click, like an old friend knocking.

choices.text: Finally trace the click to its root

effects.log: It is not the knee. It is the fear you felt falling. The body kept it for you all this time. You thank it and let it go. The click stays. You like it now.

choices.text: See a bonesetter in town

effects.log: The bonesetter is nineteen and very serious. She fixes it in one twist. The silence in your knee is strange for a week.

choices.text: Keep it as a weather sign

effects.log: It clicks. Rain by evening. It is never wrong. Better than any almanac.

events.text: A new village has a name you know. Yours. The founders were refugees you once led out of a burning valley. Their grandchildren have built a wall, a well and a very ugly wooden statue of you holding a fish. You did not hold a fish. You do not know where the fish came from.

choices.text: Ask about the fish

effects.log: The fish was a joke from the first winter, when you caught dinner with your bare hands. They remember the fish better than the fire. That seems healthy.

choices.text: Mend their wall with your own hands

effects.log: Nobody knows who you are. An old traveller who is very good with stone. They give you soup. The statue watches.

choices.text: Carve a better statue in the night

effects.log: In the morning there are two statues. The new one is much better. The village keeps the ugly one in front. You understand.

events.text: You watch rain on a pond. At twenty you saw drops. At sixty, circles. Now, for the first time, you see the pond making room for each drop before it lands. The water knows. It has always known.
events.arc: What the Rain Says at a Hundred

choices.text: Breathe with the pond until dark

effects.log: Your qi stops pushing. It makes room. Things move through you that used to hit you. You sit until the frogs come out.

choices.text: Try it in your sword form

effects.log: Your blade stops meeting force and starts receiving it. Your next sparring partner falls over and cannot say why.

choices.text: Write it down before it fades

effects.log: Five lines. They will mean nothing to anyone under eighty. You fold them into a book anyway.

events.text: A child of twelve is beating grown men with a stick at the crossroads for coins. {npc} has no style, no teacher and no fear. You have seen a dozen geniuses in a hundred years. This one makes the hair on your arms stand up.

choices.text: Teach {him} one thing, then leave

effects.log: You show {npc} how to breathe before a strike. {He} gets it on the third try. You walk away fast before you start caring.

choices.text: Give {him} money and a letter to a sect

effects.log: {npc} stares at the letter. "Why?" Because someone did it for you once. You do not say that. You say: "Eat something."

choices.text: Spar with {him} seriously for one round

effects.log: You let {him} land one blow. Then you sit {him} down gently in the dust. {He} laughs. Good. A genius who can laugh might live.

events.text: A stranger of forty kneels in your gateway with a box. {npc} says {his} great-grandfather borrowed twenty taels from you to buy an ox. The family has paid the interest into this box every year for ninety years. {He} would like the debt closed.

choices.text: Accept the box

effects.log: Ninety years of copper coins, tied in strings. You count none of them. {npc} weeps with relief and goes home lighter.

choices.text: Refuse it and tear up the debt

effects.log: You never wrote it down in the first place. {npc} does not believe you, so you tear up a blank paper. Everyone feels better.

choices.text: Take one coin and give back the rest

effects.log: "For the ox." {npc} laughs, then cries, then insists on feeding you. The ox's descendants still plough their fields.

events.text: Three blades come out of the bamboo at once. Young killers, eager, well paid. Their employer was born after your last famous duel. They have read about you in books. The books, unfortunately for them, leave a few things out.

choices.text: Fight them properly

ok.log: It takes eleven moves. The books said you used seven. You are slower than your legend. They are still on the ground.

fail.log: One of them cuts your sleeve and your arm under it. You win, but you limp home thinking about books. (-18 health)

choices.text: Disarm them and ask who paid

effects.log: A merchant's son, twenty-two, who wants the hill your house stands on. You send the killers back with a note. The hill stays yours.

choices.text: Vanish into the bamboo

effects.log: They search until dark. You watch them from twenty paces away, sitting on a rock, eating a pear.

events.text: Bandits stop your cart on the pass. Their chief is new, loud, and wears a lot of iron. The old bandits at the back have gone pale. One of them is whispering urgently in the chief's ear. The chief is not listening.
events.arc: The Bandits Know the Road, Not You

choices.text: Let the chief try

ok.log: You flick the chief's iron off one piece at a time. At the end the chief is in a shirt. The old bandits had tried to warn everyone.

fail.log: The chief is better than the iron suggested. You win, but slowly and painfully, and your purse is lighter somehow. (-15 health)

choices.text: Nod to the old bandits

effects.log: They drag their chief away by the collar. One of them bows to you deeply. You once spared his father. Apparently it runs in the family.

choices.text: Pay the toll, it is small

effects.log: Three taels. You hand them over. The old bandits look like they want to die. The chief feels very powerful. Let the chief have the day.

events.text: The ginseng you planted behind the house at ninety is ready at last. Thin white root, five-pronged leaves, red berries. Someone has been watering it while you were away. Small footprints in the mud. A child from the village, probably.

choices.text: Eat the root

effects.log: Bitter, then sweet, then warm all the way down. A century in one bite. You leave a copper coin by the bed for the child.

choices.text: Give the root to the watering child

effects.log: You leave it wrapped on the doorstep with a note: for the gardener. The village elder says the child's mother was sick. Not any more.

choices.text: Replant the seeds and start again

effects.log: Another hundred years. You might be here. You might not. The child will be. You show the child how deep to plant.

events.text: At a ferry you meet a toothless old soldier. He fought in the Red Turban War. So did you, but you were in the front line at eighteen and he was a drummer boy of nine. He is ninety-one. To him you look forty. He is sure you are lying about the war.

choices.text: Tell him the drummer boy's name

effects.log: His own name, the one his mother used. He drops his pipe. Then he cries and laughs and grips your sleeve for an hour.

choices.text: Let him tell his war, not yours

effects.log: His war has more drums in it and fewer deaths. It is a good war, as wars go. You do not correct a word.

choices.text: Share your tea and say nothing

effects.log: Two old soldiers on a ferry. One looks old. The other is old. The river does not care which.

events.text: The great river is rising. You have seen it break its banks four times. Each time the officials built the dyke higher and in the wrong place. A young magistrate, very earnest, comes to ask the famous old master for advice. {npc} has brought a map, a brush and an anxious stomach.

choices.text: Show {him} where the dyke failed before

effects.log: You draw three lines on the map. {npc} reads them twice and goes pale. The dyke is moved. The river rises, and stops.

choices.text: Go down and hold the bank with qi

effects.log: Three nights in mud to your chest. The water pushes. So do you. On the fourth morning the river sulks back into its bed.

choices.text: Tell {him} to evacuate, then go

effects.log: "Dykes fail. People run. Make them run early." {npc} does. The water takes the fields and leaves the people.

events.text: You cook for two out of habit. Two bowls, two pairs of chopsticks. The person you cooked for died sixty years ago. Your hands still have not learned. Tonight you notice. The second bowl steams quietly on the other side of the table.

choices.text: Eat both bowls

effects.log: Slowly. There is no hurry. Nobody is waiting for you to finish. That is the sad part, and also, a little, the restful part.

choices.text: Take the second bowl to a beggar

effects.log: The beggar at the bridge eats it in four bites and asks for more tomorrow. You decide to keep cooking for two.

choices.text: Leave it, and talk to the empty seat

effects.log: You tell the empty seat about the new rankings, the price of rice, the young fools in the market. It is a good listener. It always was.

events.text: A bookseller sells you a copy of your own manual. Fourth printing. You wrote it at seventy. Reading it now, decades on, you find a mistake on page eleven. A small one. The sort of mistake that could slowly ruin a student's left lung over twenty years.
events.arc: A Mistake in Your Own Book

choices.text: Write the correction to every printer

effects.log: Six printers. Four reply. Two print a slip of correction. The other two say the original sells better. You sigh.

choices.text: Write a new, better book

effects.log: A year of work. It is half the length and twice as good. It is also, you suspect, wrong somewhere you will find at two hundred.

choices.text: Teach the fix to whoever asks

effects.log: Word spreads slowly: if your left side aches, see the old one by the river. A dozen people come. Then a hundred.

events.text: A rich family has put up a stone statue of you in their courtyard, to frighten ghosts. The nose is wrong. The chin is wrong. The sword is in the wrong hand. The ghosts, the gatekeeper tells you, have not complained.
events.arc: The Statue Has Your Nose Wrong

choices.text: Fix the nose with your thumb

effects.log: Granite gives like clay under qi. The new nose is right. The family thinks the statue has blessed them. Their grandmother faints.

choices.text: Leave it, it frightens ghosts well

effects.log: You pat it on the shoulder as you leave. It looks at you with your wrong face. Whatever works.

choices.text: Ask the family to feed beggars instead

effects.log: They are astonished that the master is alive and has opinions. A rice line forms at their gate on feast days. That is a better statue.

events.text: A new sect has opened on the hill. Fresh red paint, a gate taller than the mountain deserves, a founder of fifty who calls himself the Peerless Cloud Sovereign. Their disciples bow to you on the road. They have no idea. Their founder has not come out to look.
events.arc: A Sect Younger Than Your Sandals

choices.text: Visit and drink their tea

effects.log: The Sovereign is nervous, then charming, then asks for advice. The tea is excellent. You go back every spring.

choices.text: Watch their training from the trees

effects.log: Mixed styles, borrowed footwork, one genuinely new trick with the elbow. The murim is still alive. You did not know you needed to know that.

choices.text: Leave a pine seedling at their gate

effects.log: In two hundred years it will be a great tree. Perhaps the sect will be too. Perhaps neither. Pines are patient.

events.text: On a clear night you lie on a rooftop and find the star your first teacher pointed at. It has moved. A finger's width, no more, in a hundred and twenty years. Everything else down here has moved a great deal more.

choices.text: Meditate until the star sets

effects.log: A finger's width in a century. You decide to be like that. Slow, bright, and nearly the same.

choices.text: Name it after your first teacher

effects.log: Nobody will ever call it that but you. That is fine. It is enough that someone does.

choices.text: Fall asleep on the roof

effects.log: You wake soaked in dew with a cat on your chest. It is a good morning. The star is gone, and will be back.

events.text: Another funeral this month. A friend's grandson this time, who used to ride on your shoulders. You have been to so many funerals that the undertaker greets you by name and saves you a cushion near the front.

choices.text: Stop going to funerals

effects.log: For a year you stay home. You feel better and worse. Then you go to the next one, because someone has to remember them right.

choices.text: Learn the funeral rites yourself

effects.log: If you must be at every funeral, you will be useful. Families start asking for the old one who chants slowly and means it.

choices.text: Ask the undertaker how it is done

effects.log: The undertaker, it turns out, has also outlived everyone. You become friends. You hope this one lasts a while.

events.text: A swordsman of twenty knocks at your door with a challenge letter. {npc} is the great-grandchild of a rival you beat at a festival in your youth. The family has trained for three generations for this day. {He} looks terrified and very, very determined.
events.arc: Challenged by a Grandchild of a Grandchild

choices.text: Accept, and lose gracefully

effects.log: You make it look close. {npc} wins by a hair. Three generations of grief lift off one young back. {He} bows until {his} forehead touches the ground.

choices.text: Accept, and win gently

ok.log: You win without leaving a mark. Then you tell {npc} exactly where the family style is weak. {He} writes it down, crying with frustration.

fail.log: Three generations is a lot of practice. {npc} nicks your ear and wins. {He} looks more shocked than you do. (-12 health)

choices.text: Refuse, and invite {him} to dinner

effects.log: {npc} is furious, then hungry, then confused. Over soup you tell {him} the real story of that festival. It was about a girl, and a peach.

events.text: The mountain temple below your hermitage has no bell. Its old one was melted down for spearheads in the last war. The abbot is ninety and keeps apologising to the mornings. The bronze-caster in the valley says a proper bell will cost forty taels.

choices.text: Pay for the bell (40 taels)

effects.log: It takes a year to cast. When it rings for the first time the abbot sits down on the steps and weeps. The valley hears it for ten li.

choices.text: Ring the mountain with your own qi each dawn

effects.log: You strike the great rock by the temple with your palm. It hums like bronze. The abbot is speechless, then delighted. You do this for a while. Then you pay for a bell.

choices.text: Tell the abbot silence is also a bell

effects.log: The abbot thinks about it for a day. "Very deep. Still want a bell." Fair.

events.text: The bell has cracked. Thirty winters of cold mornings. The sound is a sour buzz now. The old abbot is dead. The new abbot is a stout woman who was a novice when it was cast. She asks if you know a caster. Every caster you knew is dead too.

choices.text: Find the caster's grandson

effects.log: He has his grandfather's hands and none of his patience. You stand over him for a month. The new bell is good. He hates you a little.

choices.text: Seal the crack with qi and cold iron

effects.log: Bronze remembers being liquid. You remind it. The crack closes like a healed cut. The bell rings almost true. Almost is honest.

choices.text: Keep the cracked bell

effects.log: The abbot thinks about it. "Old things crack." It rings sour every morning, and the valley loves it more than ever.

events.text: A travelling monk stops at your door. He is fifty and was born in the valley. He says the first sound he ever remembers is the temple bell. He has walked to the edge of the world and back, and every morning, wherever he was, he woke at the hour it rang.

choices.text: Tell him who paid for the bell

effects.log: He does not believe you. Then he does. He bows to you, and then to the mountain, and then goes to ring it himself.

choices.text: Ring it together at dawn

effects.log: Two people on one log. The bell goes out over the valley like it did the first day. Some things last if you keep striking them.

choices.text: Ask what he found at the edge of the world

effects.log: "More mountains. More bells. The same mornings." He grins. You understand him very well.

events.text: A ragged orphan has started sweeping your yard without being asked. Every morning, before you wake. {npc} takes nothing, says nothing, and runs if you look. The sweeping is very bad. The yard is very clean.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of rice on the step

effects.log: The bowl is empty by noon. The next day there is a flower beside the broom. After a month {npc} lets you see {his} face.

choices.text: Correct the broom stroke, once

effects.log: You take the broom and show the stroke: from the hip, not the arm. {npc} stares. Tomorrow the yard is swept from the hip.

choices.text: Chase {him} off kindly

effects.log: {npc} goes. The yard gets dirty. You find, to your surprise, that you miss the sound of the broom.

events.text: {npc} is twenty now, broad in the shoulder, and has just come back from a sect tournament with a silver medal and a broken nose. {He} sweeps your yard anyway, every morning, from the hip. Then {he} asks the question {he} has carried for ten years: why did you never formally take {him} as a disciple?

choices.text: Tell the truth: you are tired of burying them

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a long time. Then: "I will try not to die, then." You laugh until your sides hurt. You take {him} formally that spring.

choices.text: Hand {him} your old practice notes

effects.log: You hand over a second copy you made years ago, for exactly this morning. {npc} reads the first page and sits down on the broom.

choices.text: Say a broom is the best teacher

effects.log: "That is not an answer." No. It is not. {npc} goes on sweeping. You go on not answering. You are both quite happy.

events.text: A small child is sweeping your yard at dawn. Badly, from the arm. {npc} stands at the gate, grey at the temples now, a teacher in {his} own right, watching the child. "Found {him} in the market," {npc} says. "Nobody else would take {him}." The broom is the same broom.

choices.text: Show the new child the hip stroke

effects.log: From the hip, not the arm. The child copies it. {npc} watches you both and has to look away for a moment.

choices.text: Give {npc} the broom to keep

effects.log: "Yours now." {npc} takes it like a sword. The yard is swept by another hand. That is how it goes.

choices.text: Make tea for three

effects.log: Three cups on the step at sunrise. Nobody says much. The child drinks too fast and burns {his} tongue. It is a perfect morning.

events.text: The northern tribes are over the wall again. The court calls for heroes again. The generals are making the same mistake at the same pass, again. You were there the first time, at twenty. The second, at ninety. You know exactly how this goes.

choices.text: Go and hold the pass yourself

ok.log: One old master at the narrow place. Three days. The horsemen go round by another valley in the end. The court sends a gold plaque. You use it as a doorstop.

fail.log: The pass holds, but you do not walk away from it whole. A healer stitches your side and tells you that you are too old for this. Correct. (-25 health)

choices.text: Write to the general how it went last time

effects.log: The general is twenty-nine and does not believe you. Then the first part happens exactly as you said. The second letter is read very carefully.

choices.text: Stay home. Let the young do it

effects.log: It is hard. You sit on your hands for a season. They make different mistakes this time. Some of them are better.

events.text: The sect that trained you has closed its gates. Eight hundred years, and the last elder died owing money. The buildings will be sold. A clerk asks if anyone wants the plaque from the main hall. You are, as far as anyone knows, the oldest living disciple.

choices.text: Take the plaque home

effects.log: It hangs in your small house now, far too big for the wall. Every morning you bow to it. Somebody should.

choices.text: Pay off the debts and reopen it (40 taels)

effects.log: Forty taels and a great deal of shouting at clerks. The gates open again with four disciples. Small, but the bells ring.

choices.text: Let it go. Teach its art elsewhere

effects.log: A sect is not a building. You carry its forms down the mountain in your body. Three villages learn them before winter.

events.text: Your old sect has a new sect head. You held this one as a baby, at the naming feast, eighty years ago. The baby spat up on your best robe. Now the baby has grey hair, a solemn face and a jade seal, and has invited you to the ceremony as the honoured ancestor.
events.arc: The New Sect Head Was a Baby

choices.text: Go, and bow properly

effects.log: You bow to the baby. The baby bows to you, deeper. The whole hall bows to both of you. Nobody mentions the robe.

choices.text: Go, and mention the robe

effects.log: Only to the new head, in private. They laugh so hard their seal falls off the table. Best day of their reign, they say later.

choices.text: Send a gift and stay home

effects.log: A good brush and a cake of ink. The note says: rule slowly. They hang the note in their study.

events.text: You sweep the grave of a student who died at ninety, of age, in bed, surrounded by grandchildren. A good death. You taught that student to stand at seven. You look the same as you did that day. The grave is already mossy.

choices.text: Teach the forms at the grave

effects.log: The opening form, the way you taught it then. The grandchildren watch from the path. One of them copies you.

choices.text: Plant something that will outlive you

effects.log: A gingko. They live a thousand years. Perhaps longer than you. You hope so. It would be nice to lose that race.

choices.text: Sit and tell the grave the news

effects.log: The rankings, the price of salt, a new style of spear. The grave is a patient listener, like its owner was.

events.text: A sword school in the city claims its founder was taught by you. The founder was a liar who once stole your shoes at an inn. The school is now two hundred strong, respected, and quite good. They burn incense to you every morning.
events.arc: Taught by a Legend Who Never Was

choices.text: Walk in and reveal yourself

effects.log: Chaos. The headmaster faints. When everyone calms down, you teach a real lesson. Now the claim is true. The shoes are still missing.

choices.text: Visit as a stranger and watch

effects.log: They have built a decent art on a lie and your name. It has some of your style. It has better footwork than yours. You go home thoughtful.

choices.text: Leave a pair of shoes at the gate

effects.log: The headmaster finds them in the morning, with a note: returned. Nobody understands. The headmaster, who knows the old story, goes very quiet.

events.text: Tonight is the harvest moon, one of very many. The village is making rice cakes and the children have lanterns shaped like rabbits. Nobody invited you. Nobody ever does. They think the old one on the hill prefers being alone.

choices.text: Walk down and join in

effects.log: Shy at first. Then you win the rice-cake pounding contest by a lot, and the children demand you do it again. You stay until the moon sets.

choices.text: Hang a lantern on the hill for them

effects.log: A rabbit lantern on the highest pine. The children see it and wave. The adults say the old one on the hill is finally in a good mood.

choices.text: Watch the moon alone, as always

effects.log: It is the same moon. You are almost the same person. Between you, all those years of silver light and a pot of tea.

events.text: You dream of the first person you killed. You were nineteen. You have not thought of that face in decades. In the dream you see, for the first time, how afraid they were. Exactly as afraid as you.

choices.text: Light incense for them

effects.log: You do not know their name. You never asked. You write 'the one at the ford' on the tablet. It is all you have.

choices.text: Let the fear in and look at it

effects.log: Two frightened children at a ford, each holding a blade. Your sword has felt lighter ever since, and harder to draw.

choices.text: Get up and train until it fades

effects.log: Two hundred cuts at dawn. The face fades. It will be back. Some things only open slowly, decade by decade.

events.text: Riders in black and red pass through the market. Envoys of the Demonic Cult. When you were young the Cult came only by night, with fire. These ones pay for their noodles and complain about the price. One of them has a scholar's hat. The town does not know what to do with this.

choices.text: Watch them closely, as always

effects.log: They sit straight. They count their change. Their hands are still very fast. The Cult has learned manners, not mercy.

choices.text: Sit at their table and talk

effects.log: Polite, careful, curious about you. Their leader's grandmother fought you once, it seems. They pass on her regards, and her grudge.

choices.text: Warn the magistrate quietly

effects.log: The magistrate thanks you and does nothing. Nothing happens. You are not sure who was right.

events.text: In the Cult's mountain stronghold the young believers whisper about you. You remember the Heavenly Demon three thrones ago. You remember when the Cult was forty people in a cave. A hall master of thirty, very ambitious, wants to know the secret of your long life. {He} also wants your seat.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the secret: patience

effects.log: {npc} wanted poison, or a forbidden art. {He} got patience. {He} hates it. In a few years {he} will understand, if {he} lives.

choices.text: Show {npc} why the seat is yours

ok.log: One palm, held back to a tenth. {npc} wakes up in the infirmary a day later, far more respectful.

fail.log: {npc} is better than {he} looks. You keep your seat, but you leave a little blood on it. (-18 health)

choices.text: Name {npc} your student instead

effects.log: Keep your ambitious close. {npc} bows, stunned. Now {he} must wait for your seat with good manners.

events.text: The Martial Alliance holds its great meeting in the capital. Two hundred sects. You remember when there were eleven, sworn in blood in a barn. The new oaths are written by clerks and signed with seals. Nobody has bled for anything in fifty years. You are invited as a relic.

choices.text: Stand up and tell them about the barn

effects.log: You tell it plainly. The barn, the rain, the eleven names. When you finish, the hall is silent. Then a young sect head starts to cry.

choices.text: Sit in the back and listen

effects.log: Trade routes, tariffs, a border dispute between two families. It is boring. It is also peace. You did not expect peace to be boring.

choices.text: Leave early and walk to the old barn

effects.log: It is a noodle shop now. You eat a bowl at the spot where the blood was shed. Not bad noodles. The oath held, in its way.

events.text: The sect that tried to destroy yours a century ago is gone. No war. No duel. They just ran out of disciples. Young people prefer the new schools in the city. The last old elder of that sect is selling their manuals at a market stall, one copper each.

choices.text: Buy every manual on the stall

effects.log: Their whole art for eight taels. You read all night. They were better than you thought back then. It frightens you, a little, late.

choices.text: Sit and talk with the last elder

effects.log: The elder remembers the war too, from the other side. You drink together like old soldiers. You were both so young and so sure.

choices.text: Walk past. Let it end

effects.log: Some endings belong to the people they happen to. You walk past the stall without looking back. You feel the elder watching you go.

events.text: At the wedding of a friend's great-grandchild you smell it in the wine before anyone drinks. Black lotus. Someone at this wedding wants someone else dead. Nobody here knows who you are. Two hundred guests raise their cups.

choices.text: Knock every cup out of every hand

effects.log: Two hundred cups in one sweep of qi. Wine everywhere. Screaming. The poisoner bolts and the bride's uncle tackles them. You are not invited to the next one.

choices.text: Take the jar yourself, all of it, and burn the poison out

ok.log: You draw the whole poisoned jar into your own qi and burn the poison out on the steps. The guests think you are mad. The groom's mother knows better.

fail.deathCause: black lotus poison at a wedding feast
fail.log: The black lotus is stronger than it used to be. You are not. (-30 health)

choices.text: Find the poisoner first, quietly

effects.log: A nervous cousin with stained fingers. You take the cousin outside for a talk. The wedding goes on. Nobody ever knows.

events.text: A killer drops from the ceiling of your bathhouse. A good one. Fast, quiet, poisoned needles. You learn later that the price on your head is now two thousand taels. The person who set it was born forty years after your last battle and has never seen your face.
events.arc: The Price on Your Head Goes Up

choices.text: Fight in the steam

ok.log: Steam hides needles but not breath. You hear the second needle before it leaves the hand. The killer leaves through the wall.

fail.log: One needle finds your shoulder. You burn the poison out with qi, sweating in the bath. The killer escapes. (-22 health)

choices.text: Drop under the water and wait

effects.log: You can hold your breath for an hour. The killer cannot wait that long. Eventually they leave in disgust.

choices.text: Ask what two thousand taels buys these days

effects.log: The killer, surprised, tells you: a house, a wife, a quiet life. You give the name of a good tea farm in the south. The killer goes there.

events.text: You have breathed hundreds of millions of times. This morning you notice one breath. Just one. It goes in, turns, and comes out. In it, you feel every breath you ever took, like rings in a tree.
events.arc: Breathing at a Hundred and Fifty

choices.text: Stay with that one breath

effects.log: An hour, or a day. When you stand up your dantian is deeper than it was. All from one breath, after all those rehearsals.

choices.text: Teach it to the village children

effects.log: They do not get it. Of course not. One small girl closes her eyes and sighs, and you think: maybe in a hundred years.

choices.text: Try to breathe it again

effects.log: You cannot. Chasing it makes it run. The next one will come when it comes. You eat breakfast instead.

events.text: Your sword has been getting heavier for thirty years. Not the iron. The meaning. Every cut now carries every cut before it. Young masters cut quickly. You cut slowly, and they still cannot block it.

choices.text: Make one cut a day, only one

effects.log: One cut at sunrise. The leaves on the far side of the valley tremble. You put the sword away until tomorrow.

choices.text: Put the sword away for a year

effects.log: A year with empty hands. When you pick it up again it is the same weight as when you were twenty. You laugh. So the weight was yours.

choices.text: Teach it to the strongest student nearby

effects.log: The student cuts. Nothing happens. Of course. The weight takes a century. You tell them to come back then.

events.text: A court painter asks to paint you. The emperor wants portraits of the Ten Greatest for a hall of heroes. {npc} is nervous, talented and has been warned that you killed the last painter. You did not. That one fell off a ladder.

choices.text: Sit for the full portrait

effects.log: Forty days. {npc} paints you older than you look and younger than you are. It is the best likeness ever made. You tell {him} so.

choices.text: Ask {him} to paint the ladder painter

effects.log: {npc} paints the poor fellow from your memory. The hall gets one more hero than planned. The emperor is confused. {npc} is proud.

choices.text: Send a scarecrow in your robes

effects.log: {npc} paints the scarecrow beautifully. The emperor says you look very wise. You keep the scarecrow for the next emperor.

events.text: A young physician comes to study your body. {npc} is writing a book on long life. {He} wants your pulse, your diet, your sleep and your bowels. Especially your bowels. {He} has a brush ready and is very serious.
events.arc: A Physician Half Your Age, Twice

choices.text: Answer everything honestly

effects.log: {npc} writes for six days. The book says: eat little, sleep early, worry less, train every day for two hundred years. It sells well.

choices.text: Swap: you learn {his} medicine

effects.log: You trade pulse for pulse. {npc} knows things that did not exist when you were young. You leave with a full head and a new habit.

choices.text: Send {him} away with a riddle

effects.log: "The secret of long life is not dying." {npc} writes it down very seriously, then stares at it for a long time. Good.

events.text: {npc} is two hundred and forty, a master of the Withered Palm, and once tried to kill you on a frozen lake. {He} is now your neighbour. {He} plays very bad go, cheats openly, and comes over every afternoon to complain about {his} knees.

choices.text: Play go and let {him} cheat

effects.log: {npc} wins. {He} always wins. {He} gloats for an hour. It is the best part of your day, and {he} knows it.

choices.text: Ask about the frozen lake

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "I was sure you were the one." The one what? {He} will not say. {He} only says the lake has thawed now.

choices.text: Spar, gently, like old people

effects.log: Two ancients slapping palms in a garden. It looks like nothing. The pond ripples for an hour afterwards.

events.text: A grey-haired master in fine robes kneels at your gate. {npc} was your student for one summer, eighty years ago, aged eight. {He} became a great sect elder somewhere in the west. {He} has come back to ask one question {he} has never been able to answer.

choices.text: Answer the question

effects.log: The question is about the third breath of the opening form. The answer is simple. {npc} laughs, cries, and walks home a different master.

choices.text: Ask what {he} has found instead

effects.log: {npc} talks all night. Things you never taught. Things you never knew. Your student has become your teacher. You enjoy it immensely.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep the question

effects.log: "It has kept you working for eighty years. Why spoil it?" {npc} stares at you. Then bows, and goes home grinning.

events.text: Your old sect's two senior disciples are about to fight over the succession. Both of them write to you, the eldest living ancestor, asking you to choose. Both letters are long. Both are polite. Both are full of hidden knives.

choices.text: Choose the better one

effects.log: You choose the quieter one. The louder one leaves with forty disciples and founds a new sect. In a few years they are friends again.

choices.text: Make them run the sect together

effects.log: Both furious. Both obedient. Five years of arguments. Then, slowly, they stop needing you.

choices.text: Refuse to choose

effects.log: "Decide yourselves. I will be dead one day." They do not believe you. That is the problem with being old: nobody believes you can die.

events.text: One of the Ten Greatest died this winter. Old age. The murim is buzzing. Who will fill the chair? Three names are whispered. Yours is one of them. You have been eligible, and uninterested, for decades.
events.arc: An Empty Chair Among the Ten

choices.text: Put your name forward

effects.log: The murim is shocked that you are alive and ambitious. Three challengers come to test you. None of them stay long. The chair is yours.

choices.text: Back a younger master for it

effects.log: You write one letter. The young master gets the chair. Every year they send you a crate of oranges.

choices.text: Go fishing until it blows over

effects.log: Three months on a lake. You catch eleven fish. By the time you return, someone else has the chair. Good.

events.text: Every spring the disciples of three sects walk up the mountain barefoot on the first day of the year. They call it the Founder's Pilgrimage. You started it a century ago. You had lost your shoes. You were too proud to go back for them.
events.arc: A Tradition You Started by Accident

choices.text: Join them, barefoot

effects.log: Your feet are tougher than theirs. You reach the top first and sit there grinning while the young groan up the last stretch.

choices.text: Tell them the truth about the shoes

effects.log: They laugh, then go very quiet, then decide the shoes are a lesson about pride. They keep walking barefoot. Of course they do.

choices.text: Leave shoes at the top for everyone

effects.log: Two hundred pairs of straw sandals under the summit pine. A new tradition: barefoot up, shod down. Much better.

events.text: The escort guild on the river road, three wagons and a mule when you first passed it, is three hundred people strong now, with banners, accounts and a headquarters. They hire masters by the season and run their caravans like an army. Their young guild chief, {npc}, wants you for one very important cargo.
events.arc: The Escort Guilds Are Different Now

choices.text: Take the job

effects.log: Silk and silver to the coast. Nobody attacks a caravan with your name on it. It is the most boring job you have ever done. {npc} pays double.

choices.text: Teach the escorts instead

effects.log: Two weeks with forty guards. They learn to watch the trees, not the road. The guild loses no caravans that year.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the cargo really is

effects.log: Silk, silver, and a bribe for a magistrate. You decline. {npc} sighs. {He} hoped you were old enough not to care.

events.text: A ballad singer in the market sings about how you killed the black serpent of the Western Marsh. You did not kill it. You talked to it, shared a fish, and left. The ballad has a lot of blood in it. People are cheering.
events.arc: The Dragon You Did Not Kill

choices.text: Correct the ballad singer

effects.log: Nobody wants a ballad about a shared fish. The crowd boos you. The singer bows to the crowd and goes on with the blood.

choices.text: Go back to the marsh to check

effects.log: The serpent is still there, much older, very large. It remembers you. You share another fish. Neither of you mentions the ballad.

choices.text: Pay the singer to add the fish

effects.log: Next market day there is a fish in the ballad. The crowd is confused but polite. Small victories.

events.text: A killer comes for you at night. {npc} is very young and very good, and {he} brought the wrong poison: one that was cured long ago, by you. {He} does not know that. {He} is lying on your floor now, astonished, unable to move a finger.

choices.text: Let {him} go with a warning

effects.log: You carry {npc} to the road and set {him} down under a tree. "Read more history." {He} will be back. They always come back.

choices.text: Ask who sent {him}

effects.log: A clan whose grandfather you shamed in a duel. {npc} says it with real hatred. {He} was raised on the story. You were the monster in it.

choices.text: Hand {him} to the magistrate

effects.log: Justice, by the book. You feel tired. Somewhere a clan is already raising the next one.

events.text: {npc} is back, ten years older, without poison this time. {He} has studied everything about you: every duel, every scar. {He} challenges you openly, at noon, in the market, the honest way. A crowd forms. {His} hands are steady.

choices.text: Accept, honestly

ok.log: Twenty moves. {He} is very good now. You win on the twenty-first. {npc} kneels in the dust and laughs, which you did not expect.

fail.log: {npc} draws first blood. You win in the end, barely, and the crowd sees it. {He} has learned a lot. (-20 health)

choices.text: Refuse, and buy {him} lunch

effects.log: {npc} is furious, then hungry. Over noodles you tell {him} the real story of {his} grandfather's duel. {He} does not finish the bowl.

choices.text: Tell {him} the clan story is a lie

effects.log: {npc} does not believe you. But {he} does not draw either. {He} walks away to think. That is something.

events.text: A young killer comes over your wall at night. Clumsy, loud, poisoned blade. Before {he} lands, a shadow knocks {him} flat. It is {npc}, grey now. "My student," {npc} says, embarrassed. "Wrong target. I told {him} the story. {He} did not listen."

choices.text: Laugh until you cry

effects.log: You laugh so hard you sit down in the garden. {npc} laughs too, in the end. The student lies there, deeply confused.

choices.text: Teach the student yourself, one night

effects.log: One night, one lesson. The student goes home a little less sure of the story. The feud ends the way feuds should: of boredom.

choices.text: Share a pot of tea with {npc} at last

effects.log: Twenty years of hate and then this: two people on a step with a pot of tea, complaining about the young.

events.text: A letter arrives on fine paper. It is from {npc}, who fought you to a draw seventy years ago on Thunder Peak. Neither of you has ever lost to anyone else. The letter says: "Still alive? Disgusting. So am I. Same place, same day, in thirty years?"

choices.text: Write back: same place, in thirty years

effects.log: You write one line and seal it. It is the most excited you have been in thirty years. You start training again that night.

choices.text: Write a long, insulting reply

effects.log: Four pages. Your best insults, stored for decades. You read it back and laugh. {npc} will enjoy this very much.

choices.text: Burn the letter. It is over

effects.log: You do not need to win any more. You are almost sure. The ash lifts in the wind and you watch it for a long time.

events.text: {npc} visits without warning. {He} has walked across three provinces to see if you have got slower. {He} stands in your yard and looks at you for a long time. Then {he} says you have got fat, and asks for tea.

choices.text: Pour the tea and talk all night

effects.log: You talk about the dead. All of them. {npc} remembers different things than you do. Between you, a whole lifetime comes back.

choices.text: Throw a cup at {his} head

effects.log: {npc} catches it without spilling a drop of tea. You both grin. Neither of you has got slower. Good.

choices.text: Show {him} your newest technique

effects.log: {npc} watches it once and goes pale. Then {he} shows you {his}. It is the counter to yours. You both stare at each other for a while.

events.text: Thunder Peak, a century to the day, or near enough. {npc} is waiting at the top, older, slower, burning with joy. Half the murim has climbed up to watch. They are sitting on the rocks with food. Somebody is selling pancakes.

choices.text: Fight with everything you have

ok.log: Three hundred moves. The peak loses its top. You win by a breath. {npc} lies in the snow laughing like a child. "Next time," {he} says.

fail.log: Three hundred moves. {npc} wins by a breath. You lie in the snow laughing. It is the best you have felt in fifty years. (-28 health)

choices.text: Call it a draw before it starts

effects.log: "We are too old to break mountains." {npc} looks disappointed, then relieved. You share the pancakes with the crowd.

choices.text: Fight one move only, your best

effects.log: One move each. The rocks crack between you. Nobody can say who won. You two know. Neither of you will ever tell.

events.text: A letter on fine paper, in a shaky hand. {npc} is dying. Old age, finally, the one opponent nobody beats. The letter says: "Come quickly, I want to see if you have got fat again."

choices.text: Go at once, run all the way

effects.npcPass: old age, waiting for an old rival
effects.log: You arrive in three days. {npc} looks at you and says, "Fat." Then {he} sleeps, smiling, and does not wake.

choices.text: Bring the go board

effects.npcPass: old age, in the middle of a game of go
effects.log: One last game. {npc} cheats. You let {him}. {He} dies winning, as {he} would have wanted.

choices.text: Bring the first letter, kept all these years

effects.log: "Still alive? Disgusting." {npc} reads it and laughs till {he} coughs. {He} dies holding it. Now nobody is left who saw you young.

events.text: Your sect is old now. Over supper a young disciple asks why nobody may eat radishes in the main hall. It is rule fourteen. You made it. You had a reason, once. You think hard. You cannot remember the reason.

choices.text: Keep the rule. There was a reason

effects.log: The disciples nod solemnly. You go to bed troubled. Somewhere in your memory a radish sits in a dark corner, refusing to explain itself.

choices.text: Strike it out in front of everyone

effects.log: The hall goes silent. You eat a radish in the main hall. Several elders look faint. The disciples cheer.

choices.text: Ask the oldest elder why

effects.log: The oldest elder is a hundred and two and thinks the rule is about purity of the spirit. It was not. You are almost sure it was not.

events.text: Rule fourteen has grown. The new elders have written a commentary on it: forty pages about radishes and the purity of the dantian. Two factions in your sect now argue about it. One side wants turnips banned as well.

choices.text: Remember the reason at last

effects.log: It comes back in the bath. An elder ate radishes before morning meditation in your first year. The hall was unbearable. You tell everyone. Nobody laughs. Then everybody does.

choices.text: Ban turnips too, for peace

effects.log: Both factions are satisfied. The kitchen is not. In two hundred years scholars will write books about your vegetables.

choices.text: Burn the commentary

effects.log: Forty pages go up in a bright, foolish flame. "Rules are for people, not people for rules." They write that down too. Of course.

events.text: The sect you founded has its fourth generation of disciples now. None of them have seen you fight. They call you Grand Ancestor and bring you tea on trays. Some of them think you are a story the elders made up to keep them in line.

choices.text: Give one open demonstration

effects.log: One palm at the practice post. The post, the wall behind it and the pine behind that all fall over. The fourth generation stops whispering.

choices.text: Teach the youngest class yourself

effects.log: Forty children and you. They are terrible and wonderful. One of them asks if you are really that old. You say you lost count.

choices.text: Let them think you are a story

effects.log: Stories last longer than people. You wander the halls unseen and watch your sect run itself. It runs well.

events.text: Two senior elders of the sect you founded want to divide it: the sword hall and the palm hall, two sects, two gates. Both are your students' students. Both say they are only following your teaching. Both quote you. Both quote you wrong.

choices.text: Forbid the split

effects.log: One sentence and the hall goes quiet. The sect stays whole. You know that it will split anyway, one day, after you. But not today.

choices.text: Allow it, and bless both gates

effects.log: Two sects, one root. They will compete, and both will grow faster. You visit each one on alternate months.

choices.text: Teach them what you really said

effects.log: You make them sit through a month of your old lectures. By the end they agree on only one thing: you are very boring. The split is forgotten.

events.text: You have led your sect for a century. The elders want you to name a successor, just in case. They say it very politely, as if you might break. Three candidates stand in the courtyard pretending not to listen.

choices.text: Name the most talented

effects.log: Brilliant, proud, a little cold. The sect will be strong under them. You will have to teach warmth fast.

choices.text: Name the kindest

effects.log: Not the strongest. The disciples cry with relief. The strong one leaves for a year in anger, and comes back better.

choices.text: Name nobody. You are not going anywhere

effects.log: "Ask me again in a few years." The elders sigh. The candidates relax. Everybody secretly agrees you will outlive all of them.

events.text: You realise one morning, peeling an orange, that there is nobody alive who knew you before you were famous. Not one person. The last of them died somewhere quiet, years ago, and nobody told you. The orange is very good.
events.arc: Nobody Left Who Knew You Young

choices.text: Write down who you were

effects.log: Twenty pages. The village, the dog, the first fight, the first fear. When you finish you feel lighter. Someone knows now: the paper.

choices.text: Go back to the village where you began

effects.log: It is a town now, with a wall. Nobody knows you. A dog barks at you like the old one did. Close enough.

choices.text: Finish the orange slowly

effects.log: One piece at a time. The light moves on the wall. You are still here. That is a strange and sufficient thing.

variants: Somewhere between breakfast and noon it comes to you: not one person alive knew you before you were famous. The last of them went quietly, years ago, and nobody thought to tell you. The tea is still warm. You drink it slowly.
It comes to you while you sweep the step: everyone who knew you before you were famous is gone. All of them. The last died years ago, somewhere quiet, and the news never climbed the mountain.

events.text: News from the capital: the dynasty has fallen. It is the third dynasty you have seen fall. The first went in fire. The second in plague. This one went in paperwork: a regent, a seal, a quiet abdication. The new emperor's envoy is already at your gate, wanting a blessing.

choices.text: Give the blessing

effects.log: You say something wise about rivers. The envoy writes it down. It will be carved on a stone in the capital. You hope they spell your name right.

choices.text: Refuse politely

effects.log: "Kings come and go. Mountains stay. I am trying to be a mountain." The envoy does not know whether to be offended. You give him tea.

choices.text: Ask after the old emperor

effects.log: Alive, in a country house, growing chrysanthemums. You visit him in spring. He is much happier. You both agree crowns are heavy.

variants: The dynasty has fallen, the third you have watched go. One fell in fire, one in plague, and this one in a quiet room with a regent and a seal. The new emperor's envoy is already climbing your mountain to ask for a blessing.

events.text: A shrine to you stands at the mountain pass. People leave rice cakes and pray to you for good harvests, safe births and the defeat of their neighbours. One old woman prays every day that her grandson passes the exams. She asks you, the stranger, to help her up the steps.

choices.text: Help her, and listen to her prayer

effects.log: She prays to your statue while you hold her arm. It is very strange. You decide to look in on the grandson's studies. Just a little.

choices.text: Answer one prayer, quietly

effects.log: The grandson passes the exams. He was very good anyway. The old woman tells everyone the shrine works. It does now, apparently.

choices.text: Eat a rice cake off the altar

effects.log: It is yours, after all. Sticky, sweet, a little stale. The old woman is scandalised. You do not explain.

variants: At the mountain pass there is a shrine to you, with rice cakes on the step. People ask it for rain, sons and the ruin of their neighbours. An old woman asks it every day for her grandson's exams, and asks you, a stranger, for an arm up the steps.

events.text: Two great sects are going to war over a mine. You have seen this exact war before: same mine, same two sects, a hundred and forty years ago. It ended with both sects broken and the mine flooded. The new young leaders have never read that history.
events.arc: A War You Have Seen Before

choices.text: Walk between the armies

ok.log: You stand in the middle of the field. Both sides wait for the other to attack you first. Nobody does. By sunset they are negotiating, embarrassed.

fail.log: An arrow from a nervous archer. Then a second. You hold the field, bleeding, until they stop. (-25 health)

choices.text: Send both leaders the old history

effects.log: Two copies of a book nobody has read for a century. One leader reads it. That leader's sect withdraws. The other loses the war, and the mine floods.

choices.text: Flood the mine yourself, today

effects.log: One palm on the hillside. The underground river finds the shafts. No mine, no war. Both sects hate you, together. It is a start.

variants: Two great sects are about to go to war over a mine, and you have seen this war before: the same mine, the same two sects, a hundred and forty years ago. It broke them both and drowned the mine. The young leaders never heard.
You know this war. Same mine, same two sects, a hundred and forty years ago, and it ended with both sects in ruins and the mine under water. The new leaders are young, and nobody taught them.

Two great sects mean to go to war over the old mine, and you have watched this exact war once already, a hundred and forty years ago, when it drowned the mine and broke them both. Nobody young remembers.

events.text: You have read every manual worth reading. You have beaten every master worth beating. You have climbed every mountain. Yesterday you spent the whole afternoon watching ants carry a grasshopper. You were very invested. The grasshopper got away.

choices.text: Learn the zither, from nothing

effects.log: You are awful. Wonderful. The zither master you find is a seventeen-year-old who shouts at you. You have not been shouted at in two centuries. You love it.

choices.text: Watch the ants again, seriously

effects.log: There is a whole martial art in an ant column: formation, relay, retreat. You spend a year on it. It is not a joke.

choices.text: Go somewhere you have never been

effects.log: A fishing island in the eastern sea. Nobody there has heard of you. They teach you to mend nets. You stay a season.

variants: Every manual read, every master beaten, every peak climbed. This morning you spent three hours following a beetle across the courtyard to see where it was going. It was going under a stone. You are oddly proud of it.

events.text: For three hundred years you have breathed in the mountains. Today you notice that the mountain breathes back. Very slowly. One breath in every hundred years. You have been alive for three of them.

choices.text: Breathe at the mountain's pace

effects.log: Your heart slows. A season passes in an afternoon. When you come back, moss has grown on your knees and your dantian is a lake.

choices.text: Ask the mountain what it has seen

effects.log: Ice. Then forests. Then the first people. Then you. It does not think you are important. That is the most freeing thing you have ever heard.

choices.text: Bow to it and go home for lunch

effects.log: There is no hurry. The mountain will be breathing tomorrow. So, probably, will you.

variants: After three centuries of breathing on this mountain you notice, today, that it breathes too: one long breath in every hundred years. You have been here for three of them.

events.text: The Ten Greatest meet once a decade. Nine of them are older than any dynasty. They argue about one thing all day: who sits nearest the window. The youngest of them is one hundred and eighty and is treated like a child.
events.arc: Ten Old Monsters in One Room

choices.text: Take the window seat by force

effects.log: You simply sit there first. Nobody can move you. Eight ancient masters glare at you all afternoon. The view is lovely.

choices.text: Give the window seat to the youngest

effects.log: The youngest master, a hundred and eighty, looks at you like you have handed over the moon. Allies are made like this.

choices.text: Propose a round table

effects.log: Silence. Then outrage. Then, ten years later, a round table. Nobody admits you suggested it.

variants: Once a decade the Ten Greatest sit down together, nine of them older than any dynasty, and spend the whole day on the question of who sits by the window. The youngest is a hundred and eighty and is not allowed an opinion.

events.text: The Ten Greatest must decide whether to stop a new sect that is growing too fast. It has a hundred thousand disciples and a founder of forty. Four want to crush it now. Four want to wait. Your vote decides.

choices.text: Vote to crush it

effects.log: The young sect is scattered in a season. The murim is quiet again. You wonder, often, what it would have become.

choices.text: Vote to wait and watch

effects.log: The young sect grows. Some of it rots. Some of it becomes the best school in the land. Exactly like yours did.

choices.text: Go and meet the founder first

effects.log: Forty, nervous, honest, overwhelmed. You tell the Ten: leave it alone, it will fall by itself or deserve to stand. It stands.

variants: A new sect has grown too fast: a hundred thousand disciples under a founder of forty. Four of the Ten Greatest want it crushed tonight, four want to wait and see. They all turn to you. Yours is the vote that decides.

events.text: The Heavenly Demon Cult and the Martial Alliance are at war again. It is the fifth time in your life. Both sides send envoys to the ancient master on the mountain. Both have brought gifts. Both envoys are young enough to be your great-great-grandchildren.

choices.text: Refuse both, as always

effects.log: The envoys leave together, oddly, talking. Maybe that is the only peace you can make: two young people on a road, both refused.

choices.text: Tell them how the last four ended

effects.log: Badly, then badly, then badly, then a truce nobody remembers. The envoys are very quiet. One of them asks for paper.

choices.text: Keep both gifts and send both home

effects.log: A jade horse and a silver mirror. Very nice. The envoys look scandalised. You were neutral before they were born, and you are hungry.

variants: War again between the Heavenly Demon Cult and the Martial Alliance, the fifth you have lived through. Both send envoys up your mountain with gifts, and both envoys are young enough to be great-great-grandchildren of yours.

events.text: You are the oldest living elder of the Heavenly Demon Cult. You have served under six who sat the throne. Young believers come to touch your sleeve for luck. The throne has asked you to write down the Cult's true history. The true history is very embarrassing in places.

choices.text: Write it all, embarrassments included

effects.log: The fourth throne and the goat. The sixth and the poem. You write it plainly. The scroll is sealed, and in a century somebody will laugh till they cry.

choices.text: Write the heroic version

effects.log: Fire, blood and glory. Every throne a god. The young believers love it. You keep a second, honest copy under your bed.

choices.text: Tell it aloud to the young instead

effects.log: Every night, a little more. The young listen with shining eyes. The honest version lives in a hundred heads now.

events.text: The Martial Alliance asks you, its oldest living member, to swear the new oath at the inauguration. The text has changed since your day. It is longer. It mentions trade. It does not mention the dead. You hold the brush.
events.arc: An Oath Older Than the Alliance

choices.text: Swear it as written

effects.log: You swear it. Times change. The young leaders bow deeply. They need you to approve of their world more than they know.

choices.text: Add one line about the dead

effects.log: One line in your own hand: we remember. Nobody dares remove it. In a few years it will be the most quoted line of all.

choices.text: Swear the original oath instead

effects.log: Eleven lines, from a barn in the rain. The hall goes silent. Some of the old elders mouth the words with you.

events.text: This killer is not young. {npc} is a hundred and sixty, a master in {his} own right, and has been paid by a grandson of the man who paid the last one. {He} looks at you across the moonlit courtyard and sighs. "I was hoping you had died."

choices.text: Fight. One of you will be tired after

ok.log: Long, quiet and terrible. {npc} yields at dawn. {He} bows and leaves through the gate like a guest. You sleep until noon.

fail.log: {npc} leaves at dawn, not beaten, not winning. You are both bleeding. (-28 health)

choices.text: Invite {him} to sit and talk

effects.log: Two old killers on a step. {npc} admits the job pays badly. You offer to double it if {he} goes home. {He} accepts, embarrassed.

choices.text: Ask after {his} family

effects.log: Grandchildren, a vegetable patch, bad knees. {npc} talks for an hour. Then {he} remembers the job, laughs, and leaves without drawing.

events.text: A village child tells you a bedtime story about a hero who lived on the mountain long, long ago and could split rivers. The child's grandmother says that is only a story. You live on that mountain. You split one river, once, by accident.
events.arc: Children Do Not Believe in You

choices.text: Split a small stream for the child

effects.log: The stream parts like a curtain. The child screams with joy. The grandmother sits down very suddenly on a rock.

choices.text: Agree it is only a story

effects.log: Some legends are better without proof. The child will grow up and tell it to their own children. That is the real long life.

choices.text: Tell the child how it really happened

effects.log: You sneezed. That is the true story. The child is disappointed, then delighted. You have a friend now.

variants: A child in the village tells you, very seriously, the old tale of the hero on the mountain who could split a river. The grandmother says it is only a story. You did split a river, once. It was an accident.

events.text: Young people speak differently now. The word for "strong" means "stylish". The word for "master" is used for innkeepers. Your formal speech makes them giggle behind their sleeves. A child calls your greeting "very ancient, like a temple roof".

choices.text: Learn the new words

effects.log: You call a sword stylish. A group of young swordsmen nearly die laughing, then adopt you. You are, apparently, very ancient but fine.

choices.text: Keep speaking as you always have

effects.log: A scholar comes from the capital to write down how you talk. You are, it turns out, a historical source. How flattering. How dreadful.

choices.text: Speak only when needed

effects.log: A month of near silence. You find that most things never needed saying. Your speech, when it comes, is short and nobody laughs.

variants: The young no longer speak the way you do. "Strong" means "well dressed", and "master" is what you call the man who runs the noodle stall. When you greet them properly they hide their smiles. "Like a temple roof," says one.

The young have new words, and your old ones mean new things: "strong" is a compliment on a coat, "master" is what you call a ferryman. Your courtesies make the children giggle. "Like an old temple," one says, kindly.

events.text: A monk brings you a letter sealed in a lacquer tube. It was given to his temple two hundred years ago, with instructions: deliver it to the master if the master is still alive. The handwriting is your own. You do not remember writing it.
events.arc: A Letter Written Two Centuries Ago

choices.text: Read it now

effects.log: Your younger self asks three questions. Are you happy? Did you forgive them? Is it worth it? You answer all three out loud, alone, until dark.

choices.text: Write a reply and seal it too

effects.log: You give it to the monk with the same instructions. Two hundred years. If you are alive, you will laugh at yourself again.

choices.text: Burn it unread

effects.log: Your younger self was afraid of something. You are not. The smoke goes up straight and thin and you feel very calm.

variants: A monk climbs your mountain with a lacquer tube his temple has kept for two centuries, to be given to the master if the master still lives. The hand on the letter inside is yours. You have no memory of writing it.
A monk brings you a lacquered tube his temple has guarded for two hundred years, to be delivered only if the master still lives. The letter inside is in your hand, and you remember none of it.

events.text: A young disciple bows to you on the road and recites their lineage. Their teacher was taught by a teacher, who was taught by a teacher... seven names back. The seventh name is yours. The child has no idea it is you.

choices.text: Correct one detail of the lineage

effects.log: "The third one was taught by me too, briefly. Tell the one who taught you." The child stares. You walk on. Somewhere a lineage scroll is rewritten that night.

choices.text: Ask the child to show you the forms

effects.log: Seven generations. Your art is there, under everything. It has grown things you never imagined. The child has very good wrists.

choices.text: Bow back, deeply

effects.log: The child is startled to be bowed to by an old stranger. You keep walking. You smile all the way home.

variants: On the road a young disciple bows and recites their lineage, teacher by teacher, seven names back. The seventh name is yours. They have no idea who they are bowing to.

events.text: Soldiers in the valley are drilling with fire-lances: bamboo tubes of powder that throw flame thirty paces. A general asks if the old masters fear them. A young soldier of nineteen, trembling, fires one at you as a test.

choices.text: Catch the flame and close your hand

effects.log: You fold the fire into your palm and blow it out like a candle. The general writes a long report. The soldier asks to become your student.

choices.text: Step aside and study the weapon

effects.log: Bamboo, powder, a spark. Thirty paces. In a hundred years, three hundred. You see the end of an age. You do not tell the general.

choices.text: Tell the general, honestly: yes

effects.log: "Not me. The young ones. They will die learning what this does." The general looks at the soldier, and at the tube, and says nothing.

variants: In the valley the soldiers are drilling with fire-lances, bamboo tubes that throw flame thirty paces. Their general wants to know if the old masters fear them, and a frightened recruit of nineteen points one at you to see.

Fire-lances in the valley: bamboo tubes that spit flame thirty paces. The general wants to know whether the old masters are afraid of them, and a shaking nineteen-year-old raises one in your direction to find out.

events.text: The emperor has commissioned a giant statue of you on the northern road, to frighten invaders. Thirty feet of stone. You are holding a sword you never owned, in a pose you could never manage. The invaders, reportedly, laugh at it.
events.arc: Statue on the Great Wall Road

choices.text: Fix the pose in the night

effects.log: You stand on its shoulder and recut it with your palm. By morning it is in your real stance. The invaders stop laughing.

choices.text: Leave it. Laughter is cheaper than war

effects.log: The invaders camp below it every summer and joke about it. They never cross. Perhaps it works after all.

choices.text: Stand beside it for a day

effects.log: Travellers compare you and the statue. Most agree the statue looks more like you than you do.

variants: On the northern road the emperor has raised a statue of you thirty feet high, to frighten invaders: a sword you never carried, a pose your back could never hold. The invaders, it is said, stop to laugh at it.

events.text: A scholar comes up the mountain with a long list of questions. Are you an immortal? Do you eat? Do you sleep? Can you fly? Are you, perhaps, a fox? {npc} has walked forty li and is very out of breath.

choices.text: Answer every question honestly

effects.log: No. Yes. Yes. A little. No. {npc} looks disappointed. The book is published anyway and is very popular.

choices.text: Answer every question with a question

effects.log: {npc} writes for an hour and realises {he} has learned nothing. Then {he} realises {he} has learned something. {He} goes home thoughtful.

choices.text: Fly a little, then serve tea

effects.log: Ten feet off the ground, then down again. {npc} faints. When {he} wakes, the tea is ready. {He} decides not to ask about the fox.

events.text: The well in the village below has been dry for a year. You dug it yourself, at a hundred and twenty, with your bare hands. The village has forgotten that, but it remembers you as the well-witch on the mountain, and it is very thirsty.

choices.text: Dig deeper, all the way to rock

effects.log: Down into the dark, by touch, through stone. At the bottom, cold sweet water bursts out over your hands. The village cheers for a week.

choices.text: Find the underground river

effects.log: You lie with your ear on the ground for three days. The river moved. You point. They dig. Water.

choices.text: Teach them to dig it themselves

effects.log: Harder, slower. Every family digs. Next time it dries, they will know what to do without the well-witch.

variants: The village well has been dry a year. You dug it yourself, bare-handed, at a hundred and twenty. The village has forgotten that; it remembers only the strange old one on the mountain, and it is very thirsty.

A year without water in the village well, the well you dug barehanded at a hundred and twenty. Nobody down there remembers that. They remember the odd old one on the mountain, and they are very thirsty.

events.text: In the market you see a face you know. It belonged to a swordsman you fought at forty, and to his granddaughter you met at a hundred and sixty. Now it belongs to a laughing young porter. Faces travel down the years like a river finding the same rocks.

choices.text: Speak to the porter

effects.log: The porter has never heard of the swordsman. Has a very good grip, though. You hire the porter for a season and teach a little.

choices.text: Meditate on the faces

effects.log: The same faces come round. The same mistakes, the same kindnesses. You see the shape of the river of people. It is very old.

choices.text: Buy the porter lunch and walk on

effects.log: Noodles and a smile. The face is the same and the person is new. Both things are true. You walk on smiling.

variants: A young porter laughs in the market, and you know the face: it was a swordsman's you fought at forty, and his granddaughter's at a hundred and sixty. Faces come back down the years, the way a river finds the same stones.

In the market a stranger laughs, and you know the face: a swordsman you fought at forty, a granddaughter you met at a hundred and sixty, and now a young porter with a load of melons. Faces come round, like the seasons.

events.text: A sword master you have never met defeats you in a friendly bout. Clean, fair, three moves. Afterwards {npc} bows and says {he} learned the art from a book written by your student's student. Your own art, grown up and turned around, has beaten you.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you

effects.log: {npc} is mortified. You insist. A month later you know three new moves in your own art. It is the best news in decades.

choices.text: Ask for a rematch tomorrow

ok.log: You sleep on it. In the morning you win in two moves. {npc} grins. "So that is what the book left out."

fail.log: {npc} wins again. You laugh and bow. The art has gone on without you, and that is the whole point. (-10 health)

choices.text: Give {him} your own notes

effects.log: A lifetime of corrections. {npc} holds the bundle like an egg. Your art will go further now. You will not have to carry it.

events.text: A provincial tournament is being held in town. Prize: a jade horse and the title of Rising Dragon. You are very old and very bored. Nobody has to know.

choices.text: Enter under a false name and lose

effects.log: You lose in the third round to a very excited blacksmith's son. It is wonderful. You buy him dinner. He never finds out.

choices.text: Enter and win the whole thing

effects.log: You win with one finger each round. Someone in the crowd recognises your posture and screams. You flee with the prize. Worth it.

choices.text: Become a judge instead

effects.log: You judge so fairly that three young fighters ask who you are. You say you are a retired butcher. They believe you.

variants: There is a tournament in town, with a jade horse and the title of Rising Dragon for the winner. You are very old, very bored, and very good at disguises. Nobody needs to know.

events.text: You come upon a snow lotus on the high glacier. It has bloomed once every thirty years since before any sect stood on this mountain. You have passed it four times on your way somewhere else. Today it is open.

choices.text: Take it

effects.log: It comes away from the ice with a sigh. In the valley below, it will become the most valuable thing anyone has ever seen.

choices.text: Sit with it while it is open

effects.log: Three days. A thousand years of cold, opening. It closes. You walk down the mountain feeling deeply rested.
